title: "Exercise 4.1 — One workflow, two classifiers"
output: html_document
---

*HDS MSc · Module 3 · the R version of this exercise; the web page is at <https://inflamuob.github.io/HDS_M3/day4/day4-01-frameworks.html>.*

*Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time. Keep it in the folder that holds your `data` folder. Cells with `______` are blanks for you to fill in.*

In Exercise 3.1 you predicted a number, blood glucose. Now the outcome is a
**class**: will this person have a heart attack or a stroke in the next ten
years, `yes` or `no`? The steps are
exactly the same: **specify** a model, **fit** it on the training patients, and
**predict** for new ones. Two things are new:

- the specification says the model is for **classification**;
- the prediction can be a **probability** for each class, as well as the class
  itself.

|  | Exercise 3.1: glucose, a number | Exercise 4.1: an event, a class |
|---|---|---|
| specify (R) | `linear_reg()`, `decision_tree()` with `set_mode("regression")` | `logistic_reg()`, `decision_tree()` with `set_mode("classification")` |
| specify (Python) | `LinearRegression()`, `DecisionTreeRegressor()` | `LogisticRegression()`, `DecisionTreeClassifier()` |
| fit | `fit()` / `.fit()` | the same |
| predict | a number | a class, or a probability for each class |

- **Part 1.** Predict an event from age with a logistic regression. Get the
  probability and the class for one person, see the patient on the fitted
  curve, and compare the predictions with what was measured in the test
  patients.
- **Part 2.** Add blood pressure and predict for the same person again. See
  the probability as a map over age and blood pressure.
- **Part 3.** Keep the same steps, training patients and predictors, and fit a
  decision tree instead. Follow the person to a leaf, read the probability and
  the class there, and compare the tree's map with the logistic regression's.

> **The plots are for looking at**
>
> The code for every plot is included, so that you can run it and see the figure. You are not expected to write it yourself.

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "rpart.plot"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)

theme_set(theme_bw())
```

`data/cvd_risk.csv` holds 500 adults aged 40 to 80 seen at a health check:
their age, their systolic blood pressure in mmHg, and `cvd`, whether they had a
cardiovascular event (a heart attack or a stroke) in the following ten years,
`yes` or `no`. If you do not have it yet, [**download `cvd_risk.csv`**](data/cvd_risk.csv)
into your `data` folder.

```{r}
cvd <- read_csv("data/cvd_risk.csv") |>
  mutate(cvd = factor(cvd, levels = c("no", "yes")))

summary(cvd)
```

The outcome is a factor with two levels, `no` then `yes`. The probabilities
are then about `yes`: having an event.

We split the patients into a training set and a test set, as in earlier
exercises: 80% for training and 20% held back as the test set, 400 and 100
patients. `set.seed(42)` makes the random split the same every time.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(cvd, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

count(train, cvd)
```

### Part 1 — Predict an event from age

The same three steps as in Exercise 3.1. The only change in the specification
is the mode: classification instead of regression.

```{r}
# 1. Specify: logistic regression, computed by glm(), for classification
log_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# 2. Fit on the training patients
log_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age, data = train)

# the learned parameters: intercept first, then the weight for age
log_fit$fit$coefficients
```

The two parameters are not on the probability scale but on the **log-odds**
scale: an S-shaped function, the sigmoid, turns them into a probability. Here
we let `predict()` do it.

#### Task 1a — A 70-year-old

`predict()` gives the **class** by default. With `type = "prob"` it gives a
**probability** for each class instead.

```{r}
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
person <- data.frame(age = 70)

predict(log_fit, new_data = person, type = "______")   # a probability for each class
predict(log_fit, new_data = person)                     # the class
```

> **Stuck?**
>
> The word in quotes is short for probability.

The class is the probability cut at 0.5: `yes` if $\hat{P}(\text{yes}) > 0.5$,
`no` otherwise. The red point is the 70-year-old, on the fitted curve:

```{r}
curve <- data.frame(age = seq(40, 80, by = 0.5))
curve$prob <- predict(log_fit, new_data = curve, type = "prob")$.pred_yes

ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = train, aes(x = age, y = as.numeric(cvd == "yes")),
              width = 0.3, height = 0.03, alpha = 0.3, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(data = curve, aes(x = age, y = prob), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("point", x = 70,
           y = predict(log_fit, new_data = person, type = "prob")$.pred_yes,
           colour = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Probability of an event",
       title = "Training patients (0 = no, 1 = yes), the fitted curve, and the 70-year-old")
```

> **Think about it**
>
> 1. The model says `yes` for this person. How sure is it?
> 2. At about what age does the predicted class change from `no` to `yes`?

#### Task 1b — Predictions against what happened

The test patients were not used to fit the model. Predict both the probability
and the class for each of them, and put them next to what happened.

```{r}
test_results <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(log_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(log_fit, new_data = test))

head(test_results, 10)
```

```{r}
ggplot(test_results, aes(x = age, y = .pred_yes, colour = cvd)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0, size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "steelblue", yes = "darkorange")) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Predicted probability of an event",
       colour = "What happened",
       title = "Test patients: predicted probability, coloured by what happened")
```

> **Think about it**
>
> 1. Every point lies on the same curve. What has the model got wrong for the
>    orange points below the dashed line, and for the blue points above it?
> 2. Which is more useful to a clinician: the class, or the probability?

### Part 2 — Add blood pressure

The same specification, `log_model`, with a second predictor:

```{r}
log_fit_2 <- log_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age + systolic_bp, data = train)

log_fit_2$fit$coefficients
```

#### Task 2a — The same person, now with a blood pressure of 128

```{r}
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
person <- data.frame(age = 70, systolic_bp = ______)

predict(log_fit_2, new_data = person, type = "______")
predict(log_fit_2, new_data = person)
```

> **Stuck?**
>
> The person now needs a value for both predictors. Ask for the probabilities
> exactly as in Task 1a.

With two predictors, the probability is a **map** over age and blood pressure.
The black line is where the probability is exactly 0.5: above it the class is
`yes`, below it `no`. Circles are test patients without an event, triangles
test patients with one, and the red point is the 70-year-old.

```{r}
# every combination of age and blood pressure on a fine grid
grid <- expand_grid(age = seq(40, 80, by = 0.5),
                    systolic_bp = seq(80, 200, by = 1))

prob_map <- function(fit, title) {
  grid$prob <- predict(fit, new_data = grid, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
  ggplot(grid, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = prob)) +
    geom_contour(aes(z = prob), breaks = 0.5, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(data = test, aes(shape = cvd), size = 1.5) +
    annotate("point", x = 70, y = 128, colour = "red", size = 4) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "darkorange",
                         midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
    labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
         fill = "Probability\nof an event", shape = "Test patients", title = title)
}

prob_map(log_fit_2, "Logistic regression: age and blood pressure")
```

> **Think about it**
>
> 1. The line where the class changes is straight but tilted. What does the tilt
>    tell you?
> 2. Adding blood pressure moved this person from 0.540 to 0.453, and the class
>    from `yes` to `no`. Did it change much about this person's prediction?

### Part 3 — The same steps, a decision tree

Only the specification changes. The training patients, the predictors and the
`fit()` and `predict()` calls stay the same.

```{r}
# 1. Specify: a classification tree, two levels of questions deep, computed by rpart
tree_model <- decision_tree(tree_depth = 2) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# 2. Fit on the same training patients, with the same predictors
tree_fit <- tree_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age + systolic_bp, data = train)

rpart.plot(tree_fit$fit, type = 3, extra = 106, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
           box.palette = "BuOr", roundint = FALSE)
```

`tree_depth = 2` allows two levels of questions, so the tree is small enough to
read. Without it, rpart grows 11 leaves here.

Each box asks a yes/no question. **Yes goes left, no goes right.** Each leaf at
the bottom shows three things: the predicted class, the probability of `yes`
(the share of training patients in that leaf who had an event) and the
percentage of all training patients who ended up there.

#### Task 3a — Follow the person

Start at the top with the 70-year-old with a blood pressure of 128. At each
question, go left or right. Which leaf do you reach? What probability and what
class does it give?

Check it with `predict()`:

```{r}
predict(tree_fit, new_data = person, type = "prob")
predict(tree_fit, new_data = person)
```

The same map as for the logistic regression:

```{r}
prob_map(tree_fit, "Decision tree: age and blood pressure")
```

> **Think about it**
>
> 1. The logistic regression gives every person their own probability. How many
>    different probabilities can the tree give, and why?
> 2. Compare the two maps. What shape is the region where each model says `yes`?
> 3. The three models gave the 70-year-old 0.54, 0.45 and 0.21. What does that
>    tell you?

> **Learning points**
>
> - The steps are the same as in Exercise 3.1: specify, fit on the training
>   patients, predict for new ones. For a class instead of a number, only the
>   mode in the specification changes.
> - `predict()` gives the class; `predict(type = "prob")` gives a probability for
>   each class. The class is the probability cut at 0.5.
> - The probability carries more information than the class: near 0.5 a small
>   change flips the class.
> - A logistic regression's probability changes smoothly and its classes are
>   split by a straight line; a tree gives one probability per leaf and splits
>   the classes into rectangles.
